definitions.definition: In the Upaniṣads brahman is that from which beings arise, by which they live and into which they return (TU 3.1.1); being, one without a second (ChU 6.2.1); truth, knowledge, infinite (TU 2.1.1); understanding and bliss (BAU 3.9.28); plenitude (ChU 7.23-24); the imperishable (BAU 3.8.8; MuU 1.1.5). It has two forms, formed and formless (BAU 2.3.1), and is also given only by negation — 'not so, not so' (BAU 2.3.6).

relations.note: the texts first speak of each separately and then declare them one

definitions.definition: The innermost self: the seer of seeing, not an object of seeing (BAU 3.4.2); the light of a person when all other lights are gone (BAU 4.3.6); the person made of understanding in the heart (BAU 4.3.7); the inner controller (BAU 3.7); dearer than all (BAU 1.4.8); unborn and undying (KU 1.2.18); free from evil, old age, death, sorrow, hunger and thirst (ChU 8.7.1). It is to be seen, heard, reflected on and meditated upon (BAU 2.4.5).

relations.note: identity is declared in the mahāvākyas; the later schools read the identity as strict (Advaita), as body-soul relation (Viśiṣṭādvaita) or deny it (Dvaita)

name: The identity of the self and brahman

definitions.definition: The Upaniṣads declare that the self is brahman: 'I am brahman' (BAU 1.4.10), 'this self is brahman' (MāU 2; BAU 2.5.19), 'that you are' (ChU 6.8.7 and refrain), 'intelligence is brahman' (AU 3.1.3); 'this self of mine within the heart is brahman' (ChU 3.14.4); 'the person yonder, I am he' (Īśa 16). How this identity is to be understood is disputed by the later schools (dsp:tat-tvam-asi, dsp:souls-one-or-distinct); this entry records only the statements.

relations.note: the four later-named mahāvākyas are its classic formulations

name: The four great sayings (mahāvākya)

definitions.definition: A later grouping (Advaita tradition) of four Upaniṣadic sentences, one from each Veda: prajñānaṃ brahma (Ṛgveda: AU 3.1.3), ahaṃ brahmāsmi (White Yajurveda: BAU 1.4.10), tat tvam asi (Sāmaveda: ChU 6.8.7), ayam ātmā brahma (Atharvaveda: MāU 2; also BAU 2.5.19). The Upaniṣads themselves do not use the word 'mahāvākya'.

notes: Ref correction: AU 3.1.3 is also cited as AU 3.3 (two-level numbering); both refer to the same passage.

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): the instruction (ādeśa) about brahman — 'not so, not so', for there is nothing beyond this 'not so' (BAU 2.3.6) — and the description of the self as ungraspable, indestructible, unattached, unbound (BAU 3.9.26, 4.2.4, 4.4.22, 4.5.15); akin to the negations of the imperishable (BAU 3.8.8), of the fourth (MāU 7) and 'from which words turn back' (TU 2.4).

The self who dwells in each element, faculty and being, other than it, unknown to it, having it as body and controlling it from within — the unseen seer, the immortal (BAU 3.7.3-23); 'the inner controller, the source of all' (MāU 6).

relations.note: the inner controller is the Lord seen as controlling from within

definitions.definition: That on which space is woven, described only by negations, by whose command sun and moon stand apart; unknown, all rites are finite; the unseen seer (BAU 3.8.8-11); the object of the higher knowledge and source of beings (MuU 1.1.5-7); also the syllable Om.

The culmination of Sanatkumāra's teaching: plenitude is happiness, there is none in the small; where one sees, hears, understands nothing else, that is plenitude; it is immortal and rests on its own greatness; it is all, and it is the self (ChU 7.23-25).

Brahman is bliss (TU 3.6); the self made of bliss is the innermost of the five selves (TU 2.5); 'the essence' (raso vai saḥ) — who could live if this bliss were not in space? (TU 2.7); the highest bliss of the brahma-world on a fraction of which beings live (BAU 4.3.32); the knower of brahman's bliss fears nothing (TU 2.4, 2.9).

name: The calculus of bliss (ānanda-mīmāṃsā)

definitions.definition: A graded measure of bliss: the fullest human bliss multiplied a hundredfold at each step through classes of beings up to the bliss of brahman (TU 2.8; BAU 4.3.33 with a different list), with the refrain that the learned one untouched by desire has each of these.

members: TU 2.8: human; human gandharvas; divine gandharvas; fathers of long-lasting world; gods by birth; gods by works; gods; Indra; Bṛhaspati; Prajāpati; brahman
BAU 4.3.33: human; fathers who have won their world; gandharva world; gods by works; gods by birth; Prajāpati's world; brahman's world (moderate)

definitions.definition: Beyond waking, dream and deep sleep: not inward- or outward-knowing, not a mass of cognition, unseen, ungraspable, whose essence is the certainty of the one self, the stilling of the world, peaceful, auspicious, non-dual — 'that is the self, that is to be known' (MāU 7); the measureless (amātra) of Om (MāU 12); 'the fourth is greater than these' (MaiU 7.11).

name: Waking, dream, deep sleep and the fourth

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): BAU 4.3 analyses this world, the other world, the junction (dream) and the state without desire or dream; ChU 8.7-12 leads Indra through the body, the dream-self and the sleeper to the self; MāU 3-7 names four quarters of the self — vaiśvānara (waking), taijasa (dream), prājña (deep sleep) and the fourth; KU 2.1.4 and AU 1.3.12 (three dwellings, three dreams); MaiU 7.11.

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): in deep sleep one has merged with being, 'gone to one's own' (ChU 6.8.1); one desires no desire and sees no dream, embraced by the intelligent self, beyond sorrow (BAU 4.3.19-22); one lies in the hitā channels (BAU 2.1.19); the mind overcome by light (PrU 4.6); Indra objects that there one does not know oneself (ChU 8.11).

name: The self as its own light (svayaṃjyotis)

definitions.definition: The self is the light by which a person acts when sun, moon, fire and speech are gone (BAU 4.3.6); in dream 'the person becomes his own light' (4.3.9, 4.3.14); 'by his light all this is illumined' (KU 2.2.15; MuU 2.2.10; ŚU 6.14).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): 'you cannot see the seer of seeing' (BAU 3.4.2); 'by what would one know the knower?' (BAU 2.4.14); the unseen seer (BAU 3.7.23, 3.8.11); the ear of the ear (Kena 1.2); the word sākṣin itself in ŚU 6.11 (the one God, witness, knower, alone, without qualities).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): being enters the elements 'with this living self' (ChU 6.3.2); life does not die (ChU 6.11.3); the bird that eats the fruit and grieves beside the Lord (MuU 3.1.1-2; ŚU 4.6-7); the jīva as a hair-tip part, fit for infinity (ŚU 5.9); the elemental self bound by karma (MaiU 3.1-2).

name: The two birds on one tree

definitions.definition: Two birds, companions, cling to the same tree; one eats the sweet fruit, the other looks on without eating; the one who grieves, seeing the other, the Lord, and his greatness, is freed from sorrow (MuU 3.1.1-2; ŚU 4.6-7, quoting RV 1.164.20); KU 1.3.1 speaks of two, 'shadow and light', drinking in the cave. Later schools read the two birds as jīva and Lord distinct (Dvaita, Viśiṣṭādvaita) or as the reflected and the witness self (Advaita).

relations.note: the image distinguishes two where the mahāvākyas state identity; see dsp:souls-one-or-distinct

name: The person the size of a thumb

definitions.definition: The inner person dwelling in the heart or the middle of the body, lord of past and future, like a smokeless flame, to be drawn out from the body like the stalk from muñja grass (KU 2.1.12-13, 2.3.17; ŚU 3.13, 5.8).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): the self in the form of a person at the beginning (BAU 1.4.1); the cosmic person with a thousand heads (ŚU 3.14); the highest principle beyond the unmanifest (KU 1.3.11); the divine formless person (MuU 2.1.2); the person in the eye (ChU 4.15.1).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): 'all this is to be dwelt in by the Lord' (Īśa 1); the lord of all, controller of all (BAU 4.4.22; MāU 6); the one God, Rudra-Śiva, the māyin, lord of lords, whose power is innate, who gives grace and frees from fetters (ŚU 1.10, 3.2, 4.10, 6.7-9); Indra/prāṇa as lord of the world who makes one do good or bad (KauU 3.9).

The Śvetāśvatara names the one God Rudra, Śiva, Hara and Maheśvara: Rudra is one, ruling the worlds, creating and withdrawing them (3.2); his auspicious (śivā) form is prayed to (3.5); he is Śiva present everywhere (3.11), hidden in all beings like the film on ghee (4.16), 'Śiva alone' when there is neither day nor night (4.18); the māyin (4.10).

The word appears as Indra's many-formed powers (BAU 2.5.19, quoting RV 6.47.18), as deceit (PrU 1.16), and in the Śvetāśvatara as the Lord's power: 'know prakṛti to be māyā and the great Lord the māyin' (4.10), from which the māyin projects the world and in which the other is confined (4.9); knowing him there is 'the cessation of all māyā' (1.10). Whether māyā here means the world's unreality is not stated by the texts (see dsp:world-real-or-appearance).

name: Being and non-being at the origin

definitions.definition: ChU 6.2.1-2 teaches that in the beginning there was being alone and rejects the view that being came from non-being; TU 2.7.1 and ChU 3.19.1 say that non-being was first and being arose from it; TU 2.6 says one who knows brahman as non-being becomes non-being. See dsp:being-or-non-being-first.

Brahman has two forms: formed and formless, mortal and immortal (BAU 2.3.1; MaiU 6.3); time and the timeless (MaiU 6.15); sound and non-sound, the word-brahman and the highest (MaiU 6.22); Om is the higher and lower brahman (PrU 5.2).

name: The self common to all men (vaiśvānara)

definitions.definition: The self conceived as the whole cosmos — sky its head, sun its eye, wind its breath, space its trunk, water its bladder, earth its feet — of which each partial meditation grasps only one part (ChU 5.11-18); the waking quarter of the self (MāU 3); the digestive fire (BAU 5.9).

name: The heart and the space within it

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): the self dwells in the heart, smaller than a grain and greater than the worlds (ChU 3.14.3); the small space in the lotus of the heart contains heaven and earth (ChU 8.1.1-3); the heart has five openings (ChU 3.13); from it spread the channels (KU 2.3.16; PrU 3.6); the person made of mind in the heart (BAU 5.6; TU 1.6).

name: The five sheaths (pañca-kośa)

definitions.definition: TU 2.1-5 teaches five selves, each within and filling the one before and each person-shaped: made of the essence of food, of breath, of mind, of understanding and of bliss, with brahman as the tail and foundation of the last; TU 3 reaches the same five as successive understandings of brahman. The TU calls them selves 'made of' (-maya); the name 'sheath' (kośa) for them is later Vedānta usage.

notes: Correction to the task list: TU 2.1-5 is right; the word kośa is absent from TU 2 (checked locally).

definitions.definition: Breath is the eldest and best of the vital powers, on whose departure the body fails (BAU 6.1; ChU 5.1); the one god (BAU 3.9.9); born from the self like a shadow, dividing itself fivefold (PrU 3.3-7); brahman (KauU 2.1) and the intelligent self (KauU 3.2); the gatherer into which the senses go in sleep (ChU 4.3.3); breath is father, mother, all (ChU 7.15).

Prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna and samāna are all breath (BAU 1.5.3); PrU 3.5-7 assigns them places: apāna in the organs of excretion and generation, prāṇa in eye, ear, mouth and nose, samāna in the middle distributing food, vyāna in the channels, udāna leading upward at death; ChU 3.13 links them with the five openings of the heart and ChU 5.19-23 with the five first offerings of food.

relations.note: the later yoga lists of vital currents include these five

definitions.definition: A recurring story: the vital powers (speech, sight, hearing, mind and others) dispute which is best; each leaves the body in turn and it survives; when breath begins to leave, all are uprooted, and they acknowledge breath as best (BAU 6.1; ChU 5.1; PrU 2.3-4; KauU 2.14; cf. BAU 1.3 and 1.5.21).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): 101 channels of the heart, one going to the crown by which one reaches immortality (KU 2.3.16; ChU 8.6.6); the 72,000 hitā channels in which the sleeper rests (BAU 2.1.19); 101 × 100 × 72,000 branch channels through which vyāna moves (PrU 3.6); coloured fluids and the sun's rays in the channels (ChU 8.6.1); the suṣumṇā (MaiU 6.21).

name: The sixteen parts of the person

definitions.definition: The person has sixteen parts (kalā), fifteen of which depend on food (ChU 6.7); in PrU 6 the sixteen parts arise from the person and vanish into him like rivers into the ocean, and he becomes partless and immortal; MuU 3.2.7 speaks of the fifteen parts going to their foundations.

name: Creation accounts of the principal Upaniṣads

definitions.definition: The self alone in the beginning says 'I am', divides into man and woman and emits all pairs (BAU 1.4.1-4); death/hunger at the beginning (BAU 1.2); the self creates worlds and a cosmic person whose organs become deities (AU 1); being thinks 'may I be many' and emits heat, water and food (ChU 6.2-3); non-being becomes being and an egg (ChU 3.19); from the self space, wind, fire, water, earth (TU 2.1); Prajāpati's pair of matter and breath (PrU 1.4); like sparks from fire (BAU 2.1.20; MuU 2.1.1); by tapas (TU 2.6; MuU 1.1.8).

name: Name and form (nāmarūpa)

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): the unmanifest became manifest by name and form (BAU 1.4.7); being entered with the living self and differentiated name and form (ChU 6.3.2); space accomplishes name and form (ChU 8.14); at release name and form are left behind like rivers in the ocean (MuU 3.2.8; PrU 6.5).

notes: Buddhist nāmarūpa (mentality-materiality) is a different technical sense.

name: The tripartition (trivṛt) of heat, water and food

definitions.definition: Being made heat, water and food each threefold (ChU 6.3.3); the red, white and black forms of fire, sun, moon and lightning are those of heat, water and food, and the thing itself is only a name (ChU 6.4); eaten food, water and heat divide threefold into body and mind (ChU 6.5).

relations.note: later readers relate the three colours (and the red, white and black ajā of ŚU 4.5) to the three guṇas; the ChU does not name guṇas

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): from the self arose space, from space wind, from wind fire, from fire water, from water earth (TU 2.1); earth, wind, space, water and light as the five great elements (AU 3.1.3); the fivefold quality of yoga — earth, water, fire, wind, space (ŚU 2.12); ChU 6 has a threefold scheme (heat, water, food).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): God's power hidden by its own guṇas (ŚU 1.3); the jīva bound to the guṇas and 'three-guṇa'd' (ŚU 5.7); in MaiU 5.2 darkness (tamas), impelled, becomes rajas and then sattva, with Rudra, Brahmā and Viṣṇu as their parts; MaiU 3.5 lists the marks of tamas and rajas.

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): MaiU 5.2 names Brahmā, Rudra and Viṣṇu as the foremost forms of the one, being its rajas-, tamas- and sattva-parts; MaiU 5.1 hails the one as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Rudra and all the gods.

name: Correspondences (bandhu) between body, ritual and cosmos

definitions.definition: The Upaniṣads pair items of the body (adhyātma) with items of the cosmos (adhidaivata) and of the ritual: the horse and the cosmos (BAU 1.1), the senses and deities (AU 1.1-2), mind and space (ChU 3.18), wind and breath as 'gatherers' (ChU 4.3), the fivefold (TU 1.7), combinations (TU 1.3), the person as sacrifice (ChU 3.16-17).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): time is one of the candidate causes rejected by the Śvetāśvatara (1.2, 6.1); God is the maker of time (6.2, 6.16); brahman has two forms, time and the timeless; 'time cooks all beings in the great self' (MaiU 6.14-16).

name: The candidate causes of the Śvetāśvatara

definitions.definition: ŚU 1.2 lists time, inherent nature, fixed order (niyati), chance, the elements, the womb and the person as causes to be considered, and rejects them singly and in combination; ŚU 1.3 and 6.1 answer that the cause is God's own power and greatness.

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): first taught in secret — 'one becomes good by good action, bad by bad' (BAU 3.2.13); 'as one acts, as one behaves, so one becomes'; desire → resolve → action → result (BAU 4.4.5); rebirth 'according to action and knowledge' (KU 2.2.7; KauU 1.2); conduct determines the womb (ChU 5.10.7); action does not cling to the knower (ChU 4.14.3; Īśa 2); the knots cut, actions are exhausted (MuU 2.2.8).

The Upaniṣads describe return to this world: like grain a mortal is born again (KU 1.1.6); the path of the fathers returns through rain and food (ChU 5.10.3-6; BAU 6.2.16); the self takes another body as a caterpillar or goldsmith (BAU 4.4.3-4); the third birth (AU 2.1.4); tiny creatures that are born and die (ChU 5.10.8).

name: The two paths after death: of the gods and of the fathers

definitions.definition: Those who know (the five fires) and who venerate faith and austerity in the forest go by the flame, the day, the waxing fortnight, the northern course, the year/gods' world, the sun, the moon and lightning to brahman and do not return; those who venerate sacrifice, works and gifts go by smoke, night, the waning fortnight, the southern course, the fathers' world and the moon, and return; those who know neither become small creatures (ChU 5.10; BAU 6.2.15-16; PrU 1.9-10; KauU 1.2-3; ChU 4.15.5).

name: The doctrine of the five fires

definitions.definition: Pravāhaṇa Jaivali's teaching: yonder world, the rain-god, this world, man and woman are five sacrificial fires; the offerings are faith, Soma, rain, food and semen, so that at the fifth offering water becomes 'person'; the knower of it goes by the path of the gods (ChU 5.3-10; BAU 6.2).

name: The three births of a person

definitions.definition: The first birth is as semen in the father and its placing in the mother; the second is the child's birth; the third is rebirth after the self departs at death (AU 2.1.1-4).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): the goal is named 'immortality' — the desireless knower's breaths do not depart; being brahman he goes to brahman (BAU 4.4.6); the serene one reaches the highest light and appears in his own form (ChU 8.12.3); the knower becomes brahman (MuU 3.2.9); freed from name and form like rivers in the ocean (MuU 3.2.8); knowing God one is freed from all fetters (ŚU 1.8, 6.13); ŚU 6.16 names saṃsāra and mokṣa.

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): the word is later, but the texts say the mortal 'attains brahman here' when all desires in the heart are released (BAU 4.4.7; KU 2.3.14), that the knots are cut 'here' (KU 2.3.15; MuU 2.2.8), that the best knower of brahman delights in the self yet is active (MuU 3.1.4), and 'if one has known it here, there is truth' (Kena 2.5).

Knowledge and ignorance lead to different ends (KU 1.2.4); fools in ignorance wander like the blind led by the blind (KU 1.2.5; MuU 1.2.8); Īśa 9-11 says both those who worship ignorance and those who delight in knowledge enter darkness, and that one knowing both crosses death by ignorance and gains immortality by knowledge; ŚU 5.1 calls the perishable ignorance and the immortal knowledge; what is done with knowledge is more powerful (ChU 1.1.10).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): MuU 1.1.4-5 is the root text — the lower knowledge is the four Vedas and six ancillary sciences, the higher that by which the imperishable is grasped; Nārada knows only mantras, not the self (ChU 7.1.3).

name: The last thought and resolve at death

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): 'as his resolve is in this world, so he becomes on departing' (ChU 3.14.1); 'with whatever thought one has, one enters breath' (PrU 3.10); 'mind, remember what was done' (Īśa 17); meditation on Om until death determines one's world (PrU 5); the refuge in three sayings at death (ChU 3.17.6).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): the self gathers the particles of energy into the heart, the tip of the heart lights up, and it departs by the eye, the head or another part, followed by breath and the functions, knowledge and action holding it (BAU 4.4.1-2); speech merges into mind, mind into breath, breath into heat, heat into the highest deity (ChU 6.8.6, 6.15); the creaking cart and the fruit loosed from its stalk (BAU 4.3.35-38); the inner sound is no longer heard (BAU 5.9); the breaths do not leave the dead man; the name remains (BAU 3.2.11-12).

name: Departure through the crown and the path to brahman

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): of the 101 channels one goes to the crown; going up by it one reaches immortality (KU 2.3.16; ChU 8.6.6); the person made of mind goes out through the indrayoni at the parting of the hair (TU 1.6); the self entered through the vidṛti (AU 1.3.12); through the suṣumṇā, joined with breath, Om and mind, one goes upward (MaiU 6.21); the path of the gods leads to the brahma-worlds from which there is no return (BAU 6.2.15).

The self is the rider, the body the chariot, the intellect the charioteer, the mind the reins, the senses the horses and their objects the roads; with understanding and a yoked mind the senses are like good horses and one reaches Viṣṇu's highest step; without it one goes on in saṃsāra (KU 1.3.3-9).

Objects are higher than the senses, mind higher than objects, intellect higher than mind, the great self higher than intellect, the unmanifest higher than the great, the person higher than the unmanifest; there is nothing higher (KU 1.3.10-11; restated at 2.3.7-8 with sattva).

relations.note: the top of the ladder is the puruṣa

definitions.definition: The good (śreyas) and the pleasant (preyas) both approach a person; the wise examines and chooses the good, the fool the pleasant for getting and keeping (KU 1.2.1-2); Naciketas is praised for refusing the pleasant (KU 1.1.21-29).

Venerating something as brahman or as the self: name, speech, mind and the rest (ChU 7), the sun (ChU 3.19), mind and space (ChU 3.18), the six teachers' views (BAU 4.1), 'as the self' (BAU 1.4.7); each has a stated fruit. Kena 1.5 denies that brahman is 'this that people venerate here'.

name: Powers and freedom of movement from knowledge

definitions.definition: The texts promise results: whoever venerates X as brahman moves at will as far as X reaches (ChU 7); the knower of the self's real desires moves at will in all worlds and by intention alone obtains the fathers' world and the rest (ChU 8.1.6-8.2.10); whatever world the pure-minded desires he wins (MuU 3.1.10); the self-ruled moves at will (ChU 7.25.2).

name: First signs of progress in yoga

definitions.definition: Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): ŚU 2.11 lists the forms that precede brahman's manifestation (fog, smoke, sun, wind, fire, fireflies, lightning, crystal, moon); 2.12 the body made of the fire of yoga free from sickness, old age and death; 2.13 lightness, health, freedom from craving, clear complexion, pleasant voice and smell, scant excreta.

Knowers of the self rise above the desires for sons, wealth and worlds and live as mendicants (BAU 3.5.1, 4.4.22); wanderers wander forth desiring the self as their world (4.4.22); ascetics purified by the yoga of renunciation are released (MuU 3.2.6); forest-dwellers living on alms go by the door of the sun (MuU 1.2.11); Śvetāśvatara teaches those beyond the stages of life (ŚU 6.21).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): ChU 2.23.1 names three 'branches of dharma' (sacrifice/study/gift; austerity; the student living in the teacher's house) and says the one established in brahman attains immortality; MaiU 4.3 speaks of proceeding through one's own āśramas; ŚU 6.21 of those beyond the āśramas; the fourfold scheme is formulated in the Jābāla Upaniṣad (U04) and the Dharmasūtras (U02).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): creation proceeds by tapas (TU 2.6; PrU 1.4; MuU 1.1.8-9, whose tapas is knowledge); Bhṛgu seeks brahman by tapas, 'tapas is brahman' (TU 3.2); tapas as one branch of dharma (ChU 2.23.1); the self is found by truth and austerity (MuU 3.1.5; ŚU 1.15); sickness and cremation are the supreme tapas (BAU 5.11).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): the real behind the real (BAU 2.1.20); dharma is truth (BAU 1.4.14); 'speak the truth' (TU 1.11); truth alone conquers (MuU 3.1.6); the truthful are not burned by the heated axe (ChU 6.16); Satyakāma accepted for his truthfulness (ChU 4.4); one who speaks untruth withers to the root (PrU 6.1).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): created by brahman as the power of the ruling power; nothing higher; dharma is truth (BAU 1.4.14); the three branches of dharma (ChU 2.23.1); 'practise dharma' (TU 1.11); one's own dharma lifts the elemental self (MaiU 4.3); the self is beyond dharma and adharma (KU 1.2.14).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): the self is attained by the one whom it chooses (KU 1.2.23; MuU 3.2.3); 'by the grace of the creator' one sees the Lord (ŚU 3.20; KU 1.2.20 reads 'serenity of the constituents'); favoured by him the goose gains immortality (ŚU 1.6); Śvetāśvatara knew brahman by God's grace (ŚU 6.21); refuge in God (ŚU 6.18).

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): 'to one who has the highest devotion to God and to his teacher as to God, these matters shine forth' (ŚU 6.23), the earliest Upaniṣadic use of the word in this sense; prayers and refuge in ŚU 3-6.

Lineage contribution (Upaniṣadic): Om is the udgītha and the essence of essences (ChU 1.1); all speech is held by Om (ChU 2.23.3); Om is brahman, all this (TU 1.8; MāU 1); the word all Vedas proclaim, the best support (KU 1.2.15-17); the bow (MuU 2.2.4); the higher and lower brahman whose measures lead to different worlds (PrU 5); A, U, M and the measureless as the four quarters (MāU 8-12); the upper fire-stick (ŚU 1.14); the word-brahman (MaiU 6.22).
Two brahmans are to be known: the word-brahman and the highest; one skilled in the word-brahman attains the highest; by sound alone the soundless is revealed (MaiU 6.22).

In the texts 'upaniṣad' means a secret teaching or hidden name/correspondence: its upaniṣad is 'the real behind the real' (BAU 2.1.20); the upaniṣad of the asuras (ChU 8.8.4); 'we have told you the upaniṣad' (Kena 4.7); the rule 'do not beg' is the upaniṣad of the breath-brahman (KauU 2.1). The gods love the cryptic (AU 1.3.14).

name: Teacher and pupil in the Upaniṣads

definitions.definition: The pupil approaches 'with fuel in hand' (MuU 1.2.12; PrU 1.1; ChU 8.7.2; KauU 1.1); the teacher must be learned in the Veda and established in brahman (MuU 1.2.12); pupils are tested — a year of austerity (PrU 1.2), truthfulness (ChU 4.4), 101 years of study (ChU 8.7-12); knowledge from a teacher leads most surely (ChU 4.9.3); 'one who has a teacher knows' (ChU 6.14.2); lineage lists (vaṃśa) trace teachings back to brahman (BAU 2.6, 4.6, 6.5; ChU 3.11.4, 8.15; MuU 1.1.1-2); devotion to the teacher as to God (ŚU 6.23).

name: Secrecy and restriction of the teaching

definitions.definition: The Upaniṣads restrict their teaching: Yājñavalkya and Ārtabhāga discuss karma apart, not in public (BAU 3.2.13); the honey-doctrine is for the eldest son or a worthy pupil only, not for the whole earth full of wealth (ChU 3.11.5-6); the mantha rite only for son or pupil (BAU 6.3.12); not to be given to one not tranquil, not a son or pupil (ŚU 6.22; MaiU 6.29); only to those who have performed the head-vow (MuU 3.2.10).

Several teachings are placed in the mouths of kṣatriyas who teach brahmins: Ajātaśatru teaches Gārgya Bālāki, noting that this reverses the natural order (BAU 2.1); Pravāhaṇa Jaivali says the five-fires knowledge had never before gone to brahmins (ChU 5.3.7; BAU 6.2.8); Aśvapati teaches the vaiśvānara self (ChU 5.11); Citra teaches Āruṇi (KauU 1.1); Janaka is taught by and rewards Yājñavalkya (BAU 4).
